\begin{proof}
Define $f:G\to G$ by $f(x)=x^{-1}\sigma(x)$. We claim that $f$ is injective. If $f(x)=f(y)$, then
\[
x^{-1}\sigma(x)=y^{-1}\sigma(y),
\]
so, after multiplying appropriately,
\[
xy^{-1}=\sigma(x)\sigma(y)^{-1}=\sigma(xy^{-1}).
\]
Thus $xy^{-1}$ is fixed by $\sigma$. By hypothesis, $xy^{-1}=1$, and hence $x=y$.

Since $G$ is finite, $f$ is therefore surjective. For any $z\in G$, choose $x\in G$ such that $z=x^{-1}\sigma(x)$. Using $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$, we obtain
\[
\sigma(z)=\sigma(x)^{-1}\sigma^2(x)=\sigma(x)^{-1}x
=(x^{-1}\sigma(x))^{-1}=z^{-1}.
\]
Hence $\sigma(z)=z^{-1}$ for every $z\in G$. Since $\sigma$ is an automorphism, inversion is a homomorphism, so
\[
(xy)^{-1}=\sigma(xy)=\sigma(x)\sigma(y)=x^{-1}y^{-1}.
\]
But $(xy)^{-1}=y^{-1}x^{-1}$, so $y^{-1}x^{-1}=x^{-1}y^{-1}$, and therefore $xy=yx$. Thus $G$ is abelian.
\end{proof}
